title: Towards chemistries in dynamical systems
abstract: Chemistry describes aspects of the universe in terms of molecules and their reactions. In this exploratory work we present a way to describe aspects of any dynamical system in similar terms. To describe a dynamical system in this way three decisions have to be made. The first is how many different "places" there are at which molecules or chemical species can occur; the second is how to determine the species present (or not) at each place; and the third is the set of transitions and reactions that can occur between the species in the various places. For these choices to be compatible with the state update of the dynamical system each state must be able to determine transitions that take the currently occurring molecules to those occurring in the updated state. We also propose an additional requirement that there is always a unique way to choose the least amount of transitions occurring during state updates. We discuss gliders in the game of life cellular and argue that when following their definition of according to Randall Beer they satisfy the additional criterion as well. We also point out some issues with the approach.
summary: The paper introduces 'pattern chemistry' as a method to describe any dynamical system using the language of chemical reactions and Petri nets. It formalizes this by mapping system states to counts of observable patterns (tokens). The central technical achievement is defining an 'unambiguous' chemistry, which requires that the state update must correspond to a unique, minimal set of underlying transitions.
main_problem: The work aims to develop a formal framework, termed 'pattern chemistry,' to describe general dynamical systems using terminology analogous to chemical reaction networks.
main_result: The authors propose that for a pattern chemistry to be well-defined and physically meaningful, the transition map must yield a unique minimal set of reactions required to transform the state's observed patterns from time $t$ to time $t+1$.
method: They model the system using Petri nets and token maps ($\phi$), where the state is mapped to counts of observable 'patterns' (shapes in specific frames of reference). The core method involves enforcing compatibility conditions between the source and target markings derived from the dynamical update function.
model_or_system: The general model is an abstract discrete dynamical system $(X, h: X 	o X)$. Specific examples include analyzing gliders within Conway's Game of Life cellular automaton, which serves as a concrete testbed for the framework.
key_observables: The primary observables are the 'token map' $\phi(x)$, which is a multiset counting occurrences of specific patterns (shapes) across different frames of reference at state $x$.
important_parameters: The definition relies on specifying the set of possible pattern shapes ($S$) and the frames of reference ($R$), as well as the structure of the underlying Petri net transitions.
main_assumptions: The framework is currently restricted to finite dynamical systems because multisets are defined with finite support. A key assumption for 'unambiguous' chemistry is that the minimal set of required transitions must be unique.
figures_summary: Not specified in detail, but examples involve illustrating how pattern counts (markings) evolve through specific transition rules derived from cellular automaton updates.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the general chemical metaphor for dynamical systems, then formalizing this using Petri nets and token maps ($\phi$), developing the concept of 'unambiguous' chemistry via minimal transitions, and finally testing these concepts on known systems like gliders in Game of Life.
why_interesting: This work provides a highly abstract mathematical formalism connecting general discrete dynamics (like CA) to chemical reaction network theory. The focus on minimizing transition counts for uniqueness is relevant to defining fundamental physical processes in complex many-body or open quantum systems where minimal energy paths are sought.
